PRESENTER 1 · 0:25 · OPENING

Good morning. We are presenting our Delhi Groundwater Monitoring and Forecasting System, developed as an MCA Data Science Foundation project. It turns six-hourly station telemetry into a dashboard for network coverage, station history, data quality, and cautious seven-day forecasts. We will show what the data supports, how the models were evaluated, and where interpretation needs care.

Source: Project synopsis and supplied Delhi groundwater telemetry dataset, 2021–2025.

name: section-label
text: 01  PROJECT PURPOSE

name: slide-title
text: Project problem and objective

name: problem-statement
text: Groundwater telemetry is useful only when station coverage, data quality, and forecast performance can be explored together.

name: purpose-one
text: Monitor the supplied Delhi network across all stations.

name: purpose-two
text: Inspect historical observations and data-quality flags without changing source records.

name: purpose-three
text: Compare station-level seven-day forecasts with a persistence baseline.

name: footer-project
text: DELHI GROUNDWATER MONITORING AND FORECASTING SYSTEM

PRESENTER 1 · 0:55

The project focuses on a practical problem: telemetry files are large and stations can have very different coverage. Looking at one well alone would miss the network context. The dashboard keeps all 96 supplied Delhi stations in monitoring and quality views, then makes forecasts only for series with enough usable data. The aim is not to issue an operational warning. It is to make the observations, screening decisions, and model comparisons easier to inspect.

The three goals shown here are reflected in separate dashboard views. We first look at the actual file, then explain the processing and evaluation choices.

name: slide-title
text: Data quality decisions

name: quality-description-1
text: 112,496 exact-zero readings are retained. All-zero series are flagged for forecast eligibility.

name: quality-description-2
text: Readings equal 999 are shown as placeholder candidates and omitted from daily analytical medians.

name: quality-description-3
text: Reading below −100 m is flagged and omitted from the analytical daily series.

name: quality-description-4
text: Duplicate station and timestamp keys were found in the inspected Delhi file.

name: quality-caveat
text: Screening rules do not alter the source CSV. Measurement conventions for zero and 999 still need confirmation.

name: footer-project
text: DELHI GROUNDWATER MONITORING AND FORECASTING SYSTEM

PRESENTER 1 · 1:10

The file has a high share of exact-zero readings: 112,496, or 64.98 percent. We retain them in monitoring and flag all-zero stations so they do not become misleading forecast candidates. The repeated value 999 is treated as a candidate placeholder for daily analysis, and one value below minus 100 metres is screened from the analytical series. The original records remain available. We found no duplicate station and timestamp keys.

These are transparent screening rules, not a claim that the provider has confirmed the physical meaning of zero or 999. That source confirmation remains an important limitation.

PRESENTER 1 · 1:25 · HANDOFF AT 5:00

This is the path from source file to dashboard. The loader reads only the fields needed for station analysis and caches the parsed file by its identity. We profile data quality before aggregation. For each station, available readings are summarized to a daily median; missing calendar days are not interpolated. The forecasting module builds a seven-day target, trains candidate models, and evaluates them using later dates. Streamlit presents those outputs in interactive views.

The source data stays unchanged, and screening applies to analytical series only. I will hand over to Presenter 2 to explain the forecast design and what the evaluation found.

Implementation references: app.py, groundwater/data.py, and groundwater/forecasting.py.

PRESENTER 2 · 1:10

The target is the station's daily median level seven calendar days after a feature date. The features use observations available at that date: lags at 1, 7, 14, and 28 days, trailing means, and annual calendar terms. We compare Persistence, Linear Regression, and Random Forest.

Evaluation is chronological. Earlier examples are used for training and later examples for testing. A seven-day purge removes training cases whose targets would not yet have been observed at the first test feature date. We report MAE and RMSE. Missing calendar days are not filled, and the dashboard does not display made-up confidence intervals.

Implementation reference: groundwater/forecasting.py.

title: Stations where each model had lowest MAE

text:
PRESENTER 2 · 1:30

Across 29 evaluated Delhi stations, Persistence had the lowest MAE at 26. Linear Regression was best at three. Random Forest was not best at any of the 29 stations. One of the 30 forecast candidates did not have enough dated examples for holdout evaluation. The honest result is that the simple baseline performed best most often. We do not claim machine learning improved the forecasts.

For New Delhi Mungeshpur Mungeshpur, the holdout contains 173 test targets. Its MAE was 0.073 metres for Persistence, 0.093 for Linear Regression, and 0.168 for Random Forest. These figures describe this station and test period only.

Source: outputs/model_evaluation_by_station.csv and the project's verified network evaluation summary.

PRESENTER 2 · 1:05

The dashboard brings the analytical work into seven areas. Overview summarizes the network and map. Station Explorer shows supplied observations and the station's daily history. Forecast Lab presents seven-day candidates. Model Evaluation compares actual and predicted test values with MAE and RMSE. Data Quality exposes coverage and flagged records. Insights summarizes network patterns. The Thapar Area tab adds a bounded regional bonus study.

All Delhi stations remain visible in monitoring and quality pages. A station that is not forecast-ready is still part of the network; the interface simply explains why its forecast is unavailable. The NWIC link opens the official source record, while current charts use the project's bundled CSV snapshot.

PRESENTER 2 · 0:55

For a regional bonus, we filtered the supplied statewide Punjab CSV to stations within a 25-kilometre straight-line radius of Thapar's published Patiala campus point. The app-ready subset contains 37 stations and 172,752 records, from 1 January 2021 to 22 September 2025. It supports local station histories and forecasts where data is sufficient.

The closest supplied stations are two Krishi Vigyan Kendra sensors at about 3.85 and 4.02 kilometres. The source file has no station named Thapar and no measurement identified as an on-campus well. These stations are regional context, not a substitute for campus groundwater monitoring.

Campus location source: https://www.thapar.edu/upload/files/Thapar%20SM%2030.09.2024.pdf
Punjab telemetry source: statewide CSV supplied for this project; the 25-kilometre subset is bundled with the dashboard.

name: footer-project

PRESENTER 2 · 0:20 · CLOSE

To conclude, this prototype makes the supplied station data easier to monitor and compare. Its forecasts are educational and station-specific. Before making stronger hydrogeological interpretations, we need source confirmation for measurement conventions and, for the Thapar study, direct campus measurements if they become available. Thank you.

Do not describe these outputs as groundwater depletion, recharge, safe-pumping, or volume estimates.
